turns.question: We put a pod below an old mine adit. Water is running about pH 3.2 and the conductivity trace looks wrong to me — higher than the grab samples the lab ran. Is the low pH capable of throwing the conductivity off, and if so by how much?
turns.answer:
Yes. When the water is acidic (pH < 4) the usual temperature‑compensation factors that most field meters apply can introduce a large error in the conductivity reading. The USGS notes that “the specific conductance measurement error for low‑pH (<4) waters can be large if the commonly used temperature‑compensation factors are used” and that “using the standard temperature‑compensation factors can result in κ25 °C errors as large as 50 percent”【1†"the specific conductance measurement error for low-pH (<4) waters can be large if the commonly used temperature-compensation factors are used. … errors as large as 50 percent for low-pH samples."】【6†"using the standard temperature‑compensation factors can result in κ25 °C errors as large as 50 percent, because the transport properties of the hydrogen ion are different…"】  

So the low pH you’re seeing (≈ 3.2) can indeed cause the conductivity trace to read substantially higher (or lower) than the true value—potentially on the order of up to about 50 % off.

4.3 Measurement of Specific Conductance of a
Water Sample with Low or High pH
Specific conductance (and electrical conductivity) data
are reported at 25 °C. Most modern specific conductance
meters have the capability to compensate for temperature auto-
matically. Equation 2 is used most commonly to determine the
specific conductance at 25 °C and commercially available field
specific conductance meters typically use either a constant α
(typically 0.019–0.020 per °C) or a nonlinear α (International
Organization for Standardization, 1985). Whereas these com-
monly used temperature-compensation factors work well for
waters having a pH between 4 and 11, they can be the source
of errors as large as 50 percent for low-pH samples.
4.3.1 Measurement of Specific Conductance of
a Water Sample with Low pH (<4)
The specific conductance measurement error for low-pH
(<4) waters can be large if the commonly used temperature-
compensation factors are used. To determine whether an alter-
native temperature-compensation method should be used for
samples with pH <4, the in situ specific conductance should
be compared to the specific conductance of a sample equili-
brated to 25 °C. If the measurements are comparable (within
±5 μS/cm for specific conductance ≤100 μS/cm or ±3 percent
for specific conductance >100 μS/cm), then the temperature
algorithm used is likely sufficient. If a temperature-compen-
sation factor is required for a water sample with pH <4, the
method described by McCleskey (2013) is recommended.
4.3.2 Measurement of Specific Conductance of
a Water Sample with High pH (>11)
No temperature-compensation method is available for
waters with high pH (>11); therefore, the specific conduc-
tance should be checked by making a measurement at ambient
temperature and at 25 °C for waters with pH >11. At high pH,
hydroxide becomes a major ion in the solution and its mobility
is different than that of most other ions. However, the hydrox-
ide-equivalent conductivity is much lower than the hydrogen-
equivalent conductivity and, unlike in low-pH waters, the stan-
dard temperature-compensation approaches may be adequate.
Furthermore, relatively few natural waters have a pH >11, so
this situation is fairly rare.

Check the stability of the pH meter and electrode in the

5.2 	Measurement of pH in Waters with Low
Specific Conductance
Accurate and precise measurement of pH in low-specific-
conductance waters (less than 100 μS/cm) is challenging
because (1) the water is not sufficiently conductive to complete
the electrical circuit and allow for a stable pH reading using
a combination pH electrode, (2) differences in ionic strength
between the sample and buffers are large, and (3) the potential
of the liquid junction is larger than normal. Modern reference
junctions are designed to decrease the effects of low specific
conductance, but may not always produce the desired accuracy
for measurements of pH. Low-resistance glass pH electrodes
or reference junctions with a fast, continuous leak rate can
be used to make accurate measurements of pH in low-ionic-
strength waters; however, because these electrodes are expen-
sive, generally are not designed for fieldwork, and only work
well in dilute waters, they do not replace traditional electrodes.
Some methods recommend calibrating with low-ionic-strength
buffers to minimize liquid junction potential errors, but these
buffers are easily contaminated and should be avoided in
field settings.
The recommended method allows for using normal
pH field electrodes and standard pH buffers (table 6.4–3)
by adding a small amount of potassium chloride (KCl) to a
subsample of water to increase the specific conductance by
approximately 150 μS/cm. Increasing the specific conduc-
tance by this amount has little effect on the hydrogen ion
activity coefficient; the pH is expected to be affected by less
than 0.01 pH units (Busenberg and Plummer, 1987). It is first
recommended to determine the pH by using the procedures
described in section 5.1. If the sample pH does not stabilize,
and the specific conductance is less than 100 μS/cm, then the
following procedure is recommended:
1. 	Before going to the field, prepare small glass vials
containing 20 milligrams (mg) of dry potassium chlo-
ride (KCl—crystalline, American Chemical Society-
certified). Prepare more vials than the expected number
of pH measurements. (Note: Addition of other salts [for
example, sodium chloride] also will increase the specific
conductance, but KCl is recommended to minimize
effects on the liquid junction potential.)
2. 	At the sample site, fill a 250-mL polyethylene bottle with
raw sample water. Immediately transfer 20 mg KCl to
the sample solution, cap the solution to minimize trans-
fer of gases, and gently swirl the bottle to dissolve the
KCl. Maintain the sample at ambient temperature. This
procedure will increase the specific conductance of the
sample by approximately 150 μS/cm.

5.0 	Measurement of pH
Standard procedures for pH measurement are expected
to yield accurate sample pH measurements for waters with
specific conductance between 100 and 60,000 μS/cm, tem-
perature from 0 to 90 °C, and pH from 1.68 to 10. Some of
the procedures will need to be amended to accurately measure
pH at the extremes of these ranges, but standard pH calibra-
tions and combination pH electrodes can be appropriately
used to achieve an accurate pH measurement of environmental
waters whose characteristics fall within these ranges. Studies
of waters whose properties fall outside the ranges described
above (low-ionic-strength waters and [or] waters with pH less
than 1.68 or greater than 10) require further modifications of
pH calibration or measurement procedures.
The pH of sample water should be measured in situ or as
soon as possible after removal of the sample from its environ-
mental source. The pH of a water sample can change substan-
tially within hours or even minutes after sample collection
as a result of temperature change; changes in concentra-
tions of gases (carbon dioxide, hydrogen sulfide, ammonia);
changes in redox conditions; mineral precipitation; metabolic
respiration by microorganisms; and other chemical reac-
tions, physical changes, and biological activity (Hem, 1989).
Field conditions, including rain, wind, cold, heat, dust, direct
sunlight, and direct exposure to vehicle exhaust, can cause
measurement problems. Always protect the instrument system
and the measurement process from the effects of harsh weather
and transportation damage.
In addition to potential changes in the composition of the
sample water, the reliability of pH measurements depends on
the accuracy of the calibration, and temperature measurement.
The physical limitations and characteristics of the electrode,
including response time, liquid junction potentials, and drift,
can affect the accuracy of the pH measurement.

Step 1. Calibrate the pH meter and probe (section 4.0).
Single-parameter pH meters and electrodes or multipa-
rameter instruments used for discrete sampling are required
to be calibrated on the day of use and to be checked at each
field site to ensure that the calibration is stable. The frequency
of calibration is determined by the stability of the meter.
Typically, the calibration should be done in a controlled
laboratory environment. Most modern meters have built-in
temperature compensation that works well in the temperature
range from 5 to 35 °C and pH from 4.0 to 9.5, but this assump-
tion should be checked regularly with buffers that are equili-
brated to ambient field-sample temperatures. See section 4.0
for information about and procedures for meter and electrode
calibration for pH measurements.

measurement.

adsorption, degassing, and oxidation.
• If a measurement cannot be made in situ and the

with the published data. This requirement is especially impor-

convergence or source of drainage.

3.0 	Calibration
Specific conductance measurements are only as good
as the calibration itself. Several factors must be considered
when calibrating the meter. Thermal expansion of the con-
ductivity cell can affect the cell constant; however, the cell
constants (𝐾cell) of modern field probes are generally stable
from 0 to 100 °C. Most conductivity standards are potassium
chloride (KCl) solutions, and the linear (0.019–0.020) and
nonlinear (International Organization for Standardization,
1985) temperature-compensation factors (α) will produce
reliable calibrations from 5 to 35 °C. Caution should be
used when calibrating at temperatures greater than 35 °C,
however, because the commonly used nonlinear (International
Organization for Standardization, 1985) temperature compen-
sation deviates substantially when applied to KCl solutions.
Therefore, if a modern conductivity probe that expands
minimally with temperature is used and the temperature of the
water to be measured is between 5 and 35 °C, the temperature
of the calibration solutions (either laboratory or in situ) is not
expected to significantly affect the measurement of specific
conductance of samples in the field.
Conductivity standards are susceptible to contamination
or dilution from residual solutions, including rinse water, and
each calibration should be done with care. Low-conductivity
standards (<200 μS/cm) are especially susceptible to con-
tamination. Calibration in the laboratory prior to field
measurement, for both specific conductance meters and
multiparameter sondes, is recommended because the tempera-
ture is regulated and the standard solutions are less susceptible
to contamination.
Specific conductance meters must be checked or calibrated
before every field trip to ensure that the meter and probe
are working properly. The accuracy of specific conductance
measurements should be checked in the laboratory and in the
field by conducting measurements on standards whose specific
conductance is near the expected specific conductance of the
sample. Measurements of specific conductance standards that
are within ±5 μS/cm of the certified values for measurements
≤100 μS/cm or ±3 percent of the certified values for measure-

2.2 Equipment Maintenance
Maintenance of specific conductance equipment includes
periodic inspections of meters and probes and checks on
instrument operation and performance.
• To maintain the specific conductance meter in good
operating condition—
• Protect the meter and probe from excessive heat
and cold. Keep the equipment free from dust and
transport it in a designated case for protection during
transport.
• Keep all cable connectors dry and free from dirt and
salts.
• Ensure the batteries are adequately charged and cor-
rosion free.
• Keep the probes clean. Probes may build up dirt and
corrosion that can affect measurements; therefore,
regular cleaning is required.
2.2.1 Conductivity Probe Cleaning, Storage, and
Maintenance
Accurate and precise measurement of specific conduc-
tance requires a well-maintained and clean conductivity probe.
A probe that is dirty or wet with solution other than the sample
may contaminate the measured solution and bias the mea-
surement of specific conductance. Conductivity probes must
be clean and the electrodes free from scratches to produce
accurate results. Refer to the manufacturer’s instructions for
storage and additional maintenance information.
• To clean conductivity probes—
• Clean the probe thoroughly by rinsing with copious
amounts of deionized water (DIW) before and after
making a measurement. This is sufficient cleaning in
most cases.
• Epoxy and graphite conductivity probes can be
gently wiped with a clean laboratory tissue to
remove any residues.
• Never wipe or scour platinum-coated electrodes.
• Remove oily residues or other chemical residues
with a detergent solution and then rinse thoroughly
with DIW. Probes can soak in detergents for many
hours without damage.

Combination glass bulb electrodes contain both a pH
electrode and a reference electrode. The pH electrode gener-

reference electrode generates a constant electrical potential.

when the diffusion of hydrogen ions across the glass bulb
membrane reaches equilibrium, no electrical current is present,
and the difference in electrical potential that exists between the
reference and the pH electrodes is related to the hydrogen ion
activity in the solution.

The pH of a solution changes with temperature, and most

4.1 	Calibration Procedure
The following calibration procedure is expected to yield
accurate sample-pH measurements for waters with specific
conductance less than 60,000 μS/cm, temperatures from 0 to
90 °C, and pH in the range from 1.68 to 10. Standard buffer
solutions and combination pH electrode can be appropri-
ately used to achieve an accurate measurement of the pH
of environmental waters that is within these environmental
ranges. Studies of waters with conditions that fall outside
the ranges described above may require pH calibration and
measurement modifications.

and pH Electrode used for Sample Measurement
or an Alkalinity Titration

the pH meter and electrode in a controlled environment
such as a laboratory rather than in the field. Most mod-
ern meters automatically adjust pH measurements for
changes in temperature, and these corrections are usually
accurate within a temperature range of 5 to 35 °C and for
pH measurements between 4.0 and 9.5. Electrodes may
not behave ideally, however, and this feature should be
tested regularly with measurements on buffers equili-
brated to ambient field temperatures.

3.1 	Electrode Care and Cleaning
USGS field personnel should integrate the following
guidance for the care and cleaning of pH electrodes into their
routine field-measurement procedures.
• Never handle the glass bulb with bare fingers. Oily film
or scratches on the bulb will interfere with the design
characteristics of the glass bulb membrane and affect
pH measurements.
• Inspect the electrode and electrode cable for:
• cut or frayed cable(s)
• broken connectors and mismatched or missing parts
• a visibly scratched or broken glass bulb, cracked
electrode body, and broken or damaged internal
electrodes (reference and measurement electrodes)
• a visibly contaminated reference junction
• low filling solution
• Periodically remove and replace the filling solution
• Gel-filled electrodes do not require filling and typically
require less maintenance than liquid-filled electrodes.
• Do not store gel-filled electrodes in low-ionic-
strength water, including DIW, even temporarily,

5.0 	Measurement of pH
Standard procedures for pH measurement are expected
to yield accurate sample pH measurements for waters with
specific conductance between 100 and 60,000 μS/cm, tem-
perature from 0 to 90 °C, and pH from 1.68 to 10. Some of
the procedures will need to be amended to accurately measure
pH at the extremes of these ranges, but standard pH calibra-
tions and combination pH electrodes can be appropriately
used to achieve an accurate pH measurement of environmental
waters whose characteristics fall within these ranges. Studies
of waters whose properties fall outside the ranges described
above (low-ionic-strength waters and [or] waters with pH less
than 1.68 or greater than 10) require further modifications of
pH calibration or measurement procedures.
The pH of sample water should be measured in situ or as
soon as possible after removal of the sample from its environ-
mental source. The pH of a water sample can change substan-
tially within hours or even minutes after sample collection
as a result of temperature change; changes in concentra-
tions of gases (carbon dioxide, hydrogen sulfide, ammonia);
changes in redox conditions; mineral precipitation; metabolic
respiration by microorganisms; and other chemical reac-
tions, physical changes, and biological activity (Hem, 1989).
Field conditions, including rain, wind, cold, heat, dust, direct
sunlight, and direct exposure to vehicle exhaust, can cause
measurement problems. Always protect the instrument system
and the measurement process from the effects of harsh weather
and transportation damage.
In addition to potential changes in the composition of the
sample water, the reliability of pH measurements depends on
the accuracy of the calibration, and temperature measurement.
The physical limitations and characteristics of the electrode,
including response time, liquid junction potentials, and drift,
can affect the accuracy of the pH measurement.

5.2 	Measurement of pH in Waters with Low
Specific Conductance
Accurate and precise measurement of pH in low-specific-
conductance waters (less than 100 μS/cm) is challenging
because (1) the water is not sufficiently conductive to complete
the electrical circuit and allow for a stable pH reading using
a combination pH electrode, (2) differences in ionic strength
between the sample and buffers are large, and (3) the potential
of the liquid junction is larger than normal. Modern reference
junctions are designed to decrease the effects of low specific
conductance, but may not always produce the desired accuracy
for measurements of pH. Low-resistance glass pH electrodes
or reference junctions with a fast, continuous leak rate can
be used to make accurate measurements of pH in low-ionic-
strength waters; however, because these electrodes are expen-
sive, generally are not designed for fieldwork, and only work
well in dilute waters, they do not replace traditional electrodes.
Some methods recommend calibrating with low-ionic-strength
buffers to minimize liquid junction potential errors, but these
buffers are easily contaminated and should be avoided in
field settings.
The recommended method allows for using normal
pH field electrodes and standard pH buffers (table 6.4–3)
by adding a small amount of potassium chloride (KCl) to a

7.0 	Reporting
Due to the array of reactions that can change the pH in
environmental samples, the effect of temperature on the opera-
tion of the pH instrument system, and easily changed chemical
and microbiological equilibria within the sample, pH measure-
ments are required to be completed and recorded at the field
site in situ or as soon as possible after removing the sample
from the environmental medium.
Most meters measure with precision in the range of ±0.01
units. Modern meters and multiparameter sondes can some-
times discern environmental patterns within this range. There-
fore, pH should be recorded on field sheets to ±0.01 pH units.
Accuracy of pH measurements is greater at lower values of pH
because hydrogen ion activity is greater. Accuracy of pH mea-
surements is poorer at higher values of pH because the activity
of hydrogen ions is lower.
When recording pH—
• Record the method that was used to make the pH
measurement, as well as the date and serial numbers or
other identifiers for the meter and electrode.
• Record environmental measurements on field sheets
and in NWIS to ±0.01 standard pH units, if the meter
provides this level of precision.
• Rounding for reporting purposes will depend on the
accuracy and precision of the equipment and is typi-
cally to three significant figures. Rounding to ±0.01
units at low and neutral ranges of pH, and to ±0.1 units
for pH values equal to or greater than 10.0, is recom-
mended. The accuracy and precision of the readings for
each meter should be defined further with calibration
checks and quality-control sampling.
• Always record temperature with measurements of pH.
8.0 	Troubleshooting
Consult the instrument manufacturer for recommended
troubleshooting actions for specific single-parameter and
multiparameter pH instrument systems. Many problems
encountered during pH calibration and measurement can be
attributed directly to the condition and responsiveness of the
pH electrode. Depending on use, the typical useful life expec-
tancy of pH electrodes used in environmental field operation
is approximately 12 to 18 months. With time, pH electrodes
need to be evaluated more frequently to determine whether
the deviation of the millivolt response slope falls outside the
acceptable response of 95 to 101 percent of the ideal response
slope in NIST-traceable buffers. Replace the pH electrode
when the response falls outside the acceptable range for the
response slope and the deviation cannot be corrected through
cleaning or reconditioning. Also, for any problem encountered,
first check that the instrument batteries are fully charged, and
keep spare fresh batteries on hand.
